choices: Reinstall VS Code — the keybinding is broken
Use Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) to open the Command Palette and type the command — every command is reachable by name
The feature doesn't exist — the menu bar is the only way
Edit keybindings.json to add every command manually
evidence: # developer hunting through 6 levels of menus for 'Fold All'
scenarios.hint: What's the one shortcut that finds any command by typing its name?
scenarios.prompt: What is the keyboard-first way to run any command?
scenarios.situation: A developer digs through nested menus to find 'Fold All'.
scenarios.title: Hunting through menus
scenarios.why: The Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) is VS Code's universal command launcher: type a few letters of any command — menu items, extension actions, settings — and run it without touching the mouse. Ctrl+P is its sibling for quick file opening. Keyboard-first navigation compounds: the palette removes the need to memorize dozens of individual shortcuts.

choices: Add a launch.json configuration with type, request, and program fields — the debugger needs to know what to launch and how
Debugging works without configuration — just press F5
Install a separate debugger application — VS Code can't debug
launch.json is only for Node.js — Python needs a different file
evidence:
# settings.json exists; no launch.json
# F5 prompts: 'select a debug configuration'
scenarios.hint: F5 asks for a configuration. What file defines debug configurations — and what three fields describe 'launch this program'?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and what goes in it?
scenarios.situation: Pressing F5 prompts to select a debug configuration; none exists.
scenarios.title: F5 with nowhere to go
scenarios.why: launch.json in .vscode/ defines debug configurations: type (debugger, e.g. node/python), request (launch vs attach), program (what to run), plus args, env, and preLaunchTask. F5 then starts a real debug session with breakpoints. Without it, VS Code doesn't know what 'debug' means for this project — the prompt is the editor asking you to define it.

choices: Select each occurrence with the mouse — precision matters
Use Ctrl+D (Cmd+D) to select the next occurrence, or Alt+Click for multiple cursors — edit all occurrences simultaneously
Find-and-replace across the file is the only safe way
Multi-cursor doesn't exist in VS Code — use an online tool
evidence: // rename `userId` to `accountId` in 12 places in this file
scenarios.hint: You want 12 carets, one per occurrence, typing once. What adds the next occurrence to the selection?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest in-file rename?
scenarios.situation: A variable must be renamed in 12 places within one file.
scenarios.title: Twelve edits, one keystroke
scenarios.why: Ctrl+D selects the next occurrence of the current selection, adding a cursor each time (with skip via Ctrl+K Ctrl+D); then typing edits all simultaneously. Alt+Click places cursors arbitrarily. For cross-file renames, F2 (rename symbol) is the language-aware tool — multi-cursor is for the local, mechanical case. The pattern: let the editor multiply your keystrokes.

choices: User settings apply everywhere and can't be overridden
Workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json) override user settings for that project — commit the workspace file so the team shares formatting
Settings can't be shared — everyone configures manually
The team must use the same OS for settings to apply
scenarios.hint: Two levels: your personal defaults, and the project's. Which one should the repo carry so every clone formats identically?
scenarios.prompt: How should formatting be standardized across the team?
scenarios.situation: Inconsistent formatting across the team; some have format-on-save, some don't.
scenarios.title: Everyone formats differently
scenarios.why: VS Code settings layer: user settings (personal defaults) < workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json, committed). Committing the workspace file makes format-on-save, the formatter choice, and rulers consistent for every clone — the repo carries its own editor contract. Personal preferences stay in user settings; project requirements go in the workspace file.

choices: Type the Emmet abbreviation and press Tab — e.g. ul>li.item*5 expands to the full list
Write all the HTML by hand — abbreviations are unreliable
Emmet only works in .html files — not in JSX
Install a separate Emmet extension — it's not built in
scenarios.hint: `ul>li.item*5` is a tiny language for HTML structure. What key expands it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you generate the markup quickly?
scenarios.situation: A developer hand-writes repetitive HTML lists.
scenarios.title: The unexpanded abbreviation
scenarios.why: Emmet is built into VS Code: CSS-like abbreviations (ul>li.item*5, div.container>header+main+footer) expand with Tab into full markup, including numbering ($), attributes, and lorem text. It works in HTML, JSX, and more. Hand-writing repetitive structure is the slowest possible approach to a solved problem.

choices: Reload the window — the extension activates eventually
Check the extension's requirements: many language extensions need a language server binary, SDK, or runtime installed separately (e.g., Python interpreter, .NET SDK)
Extensions always work out of the box — the code must be wrong
Uninstall and reinstall VS Code — the extension host is corrupted
evidence: # installed 'Python' extension; no IntelliSense, no 'Run Python File'
scenarios.hint: The extension is a client; who does the actual language work — and is that piece installed?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the extension inert?
scenarios.situation: A language extension installs but provides no features.
scenarios.title: The extension that does nothing
scenarios.why: Most language extensions are front-ends for a language server, SDK, or runtime that must exist separately — the Python extension needs a Python interpreter selected, C# needs the .NET SDK, Java needs a JDK. The extension contributes UI; the toolchain does the work. First check in the extension's docs: 'Requirements'. Installing the UI without the engine is the classic empty-extension experience.

choices: Use find-and-replace across the project — fastest
Place the caret on the symbol and press Shift+F6 (Rename refactoring) — updates all references safely, respecting scope
Rename the file — the class follows automatically
Rename only the declaration — references update themselves
scenarios.hint: Find-and-replace can't tell a class name from a comment containing the same word. What refactoring understands scope and references?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rename?
scenarios.situation: A class used in 40 files must be renamed.
scenarios.title: Renaming across forty files
scenarios.why: Shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed. Find-and-replace is textual and blind. The IDE's refactoring engine exists precisely so renames are safe, previewable operations, not hope-driven edits.

choices: Open the file in the editor first — there's no global search
Press Shift twice (Search Everywhere) or Ctrl+Shift+F (Find in Path) — search classes, files, symbols, and text across the project
Use the OS file search — the IDE can't search contents
Grep in the terminal — the IDE has no search
evidence: # where is `calculateTax` defined? which files reference the `discount` field?
scenarios.hint: You need to find a symbol by name and text across the whole project. What searches everything — files, classes, actions — from one box?
scenarios.prompt: How do you locate the symbol and its usages?
scenarios.situation: A developer browses the project tree looking for a method definition.
scenarios.title: Browsing instead of searching
scenarios.why: Search Everywhere (double-Shift) finds classes, files, symbols, and IDE actions by name; Find in Path (Ctrl+Shift+F) searches file contents with regex and scope filters; Alt+F7 finds usages of the symbol at the caret. Tree-browsing is linear; search is indexed. Professional IDE fluency is largely navigation fluency.

choices: Add print statements — the debugger is too slow for this
Set a breakpoint (Ctrl+F8), run in Debug mode, and use Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) plus Watches to inspect state — no code changes needed
The debugger can't inspect variables — only the console can
Restart the app with more logging and redeploy
evidence: # intermittent wrong total in a 200-line calculation; prints would take hours
scenarios.hint: You need to see variable values at a specific line, on demand, without editing code. What pauses execution and lets you interrogate state?
scenarios.prompt: What is the efficient approach?
scenarios.situation: An intermittent wrong total in a long calculation; print-debugging would take hours.
scenarios.title: Interrogating the running program
scenarios.why: The debugger pauses at breakpoints and lets you inspect the full state: Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) runs arbitrary expressions in the current frame, Watches track values across steps, and conditional breakpoints stop only on the failing case. Print-debugging edits code, rebuilds, and reruns per hypothesis — the debugger tests hypotheses in seconds without touching the source.

choices: Delete the method and rewrite it — extraction is manual
Select the block and use Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M) — the IDE creates the method, infers parameters and return, and replaces the block with a call
Copy-paste into a new method and fix the references by hand
Long methods are fine — extraction hurts readability
evidence: // 60-line method; a 15-line block is copy-pasted in 3 places
scenarios.hint: The IDE can carve a method out of selected code. What does it infer — parameters in, value out?
scenarios.prompt: How should the duplication be removed?
scenarios.situation: A 15-line block is duplicated in three places inside a long method.
scenarios.title: The tripled block
scenarios.why: Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M) analyzes the selection, infers parameters (values read) and return (value written), creates the method, and replaces each copy with a call. Manual extraction risks missing a variable or mis-wiring a parameter; the refactoring is provably behavior-preserving. Duplicated blocks are the canonical extract-method trigger.

choices: Run configurations are fixed — one per project
Create a run configuration (Run > Edit Configurations) with the right main class/script, arguments, and environment — configurations are shareable via .run/ or versioned files
The IDE always runs the currently open file — that's the only option
Run configurations can't take arguments — hardcode them
evidence: # app needs --port 8081 and ENV=staging to run locally
scenarios.hint: Running needs more than 'press play': arguments, env vars, working directory. Where does the IDE store a named, repeatable launch?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the launch repeatable?
scenarios.situation: Local runs need specific args and env vars; the developer retypes them each time.
scenarios.title: Retyping the launch
scenarios.why: Run configurations capture the launch recipe — main class/script, program arguments, environment variables, working directory — as a named, one-click (and debuggable) entry. They can be shared with the team via versioned files. Retyping args per launch is slow and error-prone; the configuration makes 'how do I run this' a stored answer.

choices: Press Alt+Enter on the warning — intention actions offer the fix (add import, create method, suppress with justification) right at the caret
Ignore all warnings — they're just style opinions
Warnings can't be fixed in bulk — each needs manual editing
Disable inspections entirely — they slow down the IDE
evidence: // IDE highlights: 'Method can be static', 'Unused import', 'Possible NPE'
scenarios.hint: The IDE already knows what's wrong — and usually knows the fix. What key asks it 'what can you do here?'
scenarios.prompt: How should the warnings be handled?
scenarios.situation: The IDE highlights several warnings; the developer isn't sure what to do about them.
scenarios.title: The yellow squiggles
scenarios.why: Alt+Enter (Show Intention Actions) is the IDE's 'fix it for me' key: it offers the applicable quick-fix at the caret — organize imports, generate the missing method, apply the suggested refactoring. Inspections are continuous static analysis; intentions are their actionable front-end. Ignoring them wastes the analysis; the workflow is: read the warning, Alt+Enter, accept or deliberately suppress.

choices: F5 always starts without the debugger — that's its purpose
F5 starts debugging (debugger attached); Ctrl+F5 starts without debugging — pick based on whether you need breakpoints
Both do the same thing — the difference is historical
F5 is for web apps only; console apps need Ctrl+F5
evidence: # developer presses F5 to 'just run' and wonders why it's slow
scenarios.hint: One attaches the debugger (breakpoints work, slower); the other just runs. Which is which?
scenarios.prompt: What is the difference, and when do you use each?
scenarios.situation: A developer always presses F5 to run and complains it's slow.
scenarios.title: Always debugging
scenarios.why: F5 = Start Debugging (debugger attached: breakpoints, variable inspection, slower startup); Ctrl+F5 = Start Without Debugging (just runs). If you're not debugging, Ctrl+F5 skips the debugger overhead. The choice is intent: investigating → F5; smoke-testing a run → Ctrl+F5.

choices: Use Debug > Attach to Process, select the running process — the debugger attaches to the live process with its symbols
You can't debug a running process — restart it under F5
Attach to Process only works for web apps
Copy the PDBs to the desktop — the debugger finds them there
evidence: # service running in production-like staging; bug only reproduces there
scenarios.hint: The process is already running and you can't restart it. What debugger feature joins a live process?
scenarios.prompt: How do you debug the running service?
scenarios.situation: A bug reproduces only in the long-running staging service; restarting loses the state.
scenarios.title: Debugging the unrestartable
scenarios.why: Attach to Process connects the debugger to an already-running process — breakpoints hit in the live service, with call stacks and variable inspection. Requirements: matching symbols (PDBs) and appropriate permissions. Restart-under-F5 is the common case; attach is the tool for 'it only happens after three hours of uptime'.

choices: The Immediate Window only runs in Release builds
Open the Immediate Window (Debug > Windows > Immediate) during a debug session and evaluate expressions / call methods in the current context
Immediate Window is a text editor — it can't execute code
You must add a Watch for every expression — the Immediate Window is read-only
evidence: # paused at a breakpoint; want to test `order.ApplyDiscount(0.1)` without editing code
scenarios.hint: You're paused in the debugger with full context. What window lets you type and execute code right there?
scenarios.prompt: How do you try the expression live?
scenarios.situation: Paused at a breakpoint, the developer wants to test a method call against the live state.
scenarios.title: The live experiment
scenarios.why: The Immediate Window evaluates expressions and statements in the paused program's context — call methods, inspect objects, even assign variables to steer the session. It's the debugger's REPL: test hypotheses (does ApplyDiscount fix the total?) without editing, rebuilding, and rerunning. Watches observe; the Immediate Window experiments.

choices: Reference the DLL by copying it into bin/ — simplest
Use the NuGet Package Manager (or dotnet add package) to add the versioned package reference — restorable, versioned, transitive
NuGet is only for Microsoft packages — third-party needs manual DLLs
Edit the .csproj by hand to add a HintPath — the modern approach
scenarios.hint: Manual DLLs don't restore on a fresh clone. What mechanism versions, restores, and transitively resolves dependencies?
scenarios.prompt: How should the dependency be added?
scenarios.situation: A developer copies a DLL into the project to use a JSON library.
scenarios.title: The DLL in the repo
scenarios.why: NuGet package references (<PackageReference> in the SDK-style csproj) are versioned, restorable (dotnet restore fetches them on any machine), and transitive — the package's own dependencies resolve automatically. Committed DLLs rot (which version? where from?), don't restore, and hide transitive needs. The Package Manager UI or dotnet add package is the one correct path.

choices: Build the solution in the Release configuration — Debug builds can't be deployed
Build configurations (Debug/Release) control symbols, optimizations, and conditional compilation — develop in Debug, ship Release
Configurations are just names — they change nothing
Always ship Debug — it has more diagnostics
scenarios.hint: What differs between the two besides the name — optimizations? symbols? What should production get?
scenarios.prompt: What do the configurations control?
scenarios.situation: A developer ships the Debug build to staging 'because it has better error messages'.
scenarios.title: Debug in staging
scenarios.why: Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance. Shipping Debug to production-adjacent environments is slower and can behave differently (timing, inlining). The dropdown also drives conditional compilation (#if DEBUG) — diagnostics code that must never ship.

choices: The .sln file lists every source file — edit it to add the class
Add the existing file to the project (or ensure SDK-style globbing includes it) — the project file defines membership; the solution just groups projects
Source files are auto-discovered — no action ever needed
Create a new solution per file — solutions can't share projects
evidence: # added Helper.cs to the folder; it doesn't compile ('type not found')
scenarios.hint: The file exists on disk but the compiler doesn't see it. What declares 'these files belong to this project'?
scenarios.prompt: Why doesn't the new file compile?
scenarios.situation: A .cs file added to the folder isn't compiled.
scenarios.title: The file the compiler can't see
scenarios.why: The project file (.csproj) defines compilation membership; the solution (.sln) merely groups projects. SDK-style projects glob *.cs automatically (so this usually just works), but classic/legacy projects list files explicitly — a disk file isn't a project file until added. 'Type not found' for a file sitting right there is almost always a membership problem.

choices: Start changing code immediately — action beats analysis
Reproduce the bug reliably first (minimal repro), then form a hypothesis, test it, and only then change code — debugging is the scientific method
Read the entire codebase — understanding everything precedes any fix
Ask a teammate to fix it — fresh eyes are the method
evidence: # 'sometimes the total is wrong' — no repro steps
scenarios.hint: You can't verify a fix for something you can't trigger. What's the first deliverable of any debugging session?
scenarios.prompt: What is the first step?
scenarios.situation: A bug report says 'sometimes the total is wrong' with no steps.
scenarios.title: The unreproducible bug
scenarios.why: A reliable reproduction is the foundation: it turns 'sometimes' into a deterministic trigger, gives you a before/after oracle for the fix, and often reveals the cause while you minimize it. Code changes before reproduction are guesses. The workflow — reproduce, hypothesize, instrument, verify — is what separates debugging from flailing.

choices: Add a conditional breakpoint (or logpoint) that only triggers on the failing case — inspect the exact failing state without stopping 10,000 good iterations
Set a breakpoint at the loop start and press F5 10,000 times
Add a Console.WriteLine and rerun — prints are the only way
Give up — intermittent bugs can't be debugged
evidence: # loop of 10,000 orders; order #7,431 computes the wrong total
scenarios.hint: You need to stop exactly when order #7,431 processes. What breakpoint feature filters by condition — without code changes?
scenarios.prompt: How do you catch the one failing iteration?
scenarios.situation: One iteration in 10,000 computes wrong; a plain breakpoint would stop 7,431 times.
scenarios.title: The one bad iteration
scenarios.why: Conditional breakpoints (break when order.Id == 7431, or when total < 0) stop only on the failing case; logpoints ('logpoints'/'tracepoints') print values without stopping at all. Both inspect production-fidelity state with zero code changes. Print-debugging the loop means editing, rebuilding, and drowning in 10,000 lines — the debugger filters at the source.

choices: The bug is in the code you wrote most recently — always
Bisect: check the behavior at the midpoint of the suspect range (git bisect for regressions, or halve the input), discard the innocent half, repeat — logarithmic narrowing
Read the code top to bottom until the bug appears
Add logging everywhere at once — coverage beats precision
evidence: # worked in v2.3, broken in v2.4 — 300 commits in between
scenarios.hint: 300 suspects. What's the fastest way to find the guilty commit — check them one by one, or halve the range each time?
scenarios.prompt: How do you find the breaking change?
scenarios.situation: A regression appeared somewhere in 300 commits.
scenarios.title: Three hundred suspects
scenarios.why: Bisection is binary search on history: git bisect checks the midpoint commit, marks good/bad, and halves the range — ~9 steps for 300 commits instead of 300. The same halving applies to inputs and code paths. It's the optimal strategy whenever you have an orderable range and a pass/fail oracle. Linear scanning is the fallback, not the plan.

choices: Explain it to a rubber duck (or a teammate, or write it up) — articulating the assumptions exposes the false one
Stare at the code harder — focus finds bugs
Take a week off — distance is the only fix
Rewrite the module — the bug won't survive a rewrite
evidence: # 3 hours stuck; the bug was a wrong variable name, invisible to the author
scenarios.hint: You've read the code ten times and see what you expect. What forces you to confront what the code actually says?
scenarios.prompt: What technique breaks the impasse?
scenarios.situation: Three hours stuck on a bug that turned out to be a wrong variable name.
scenarios.title: Stuck for three hours
scenarios.why: Rubber-duck debugging works because explaining forces precision: 'this variable holds the user id' — wait, does it? The act of articulating each assumption exposes the false one your eyes skipped. Writing the Stack Overflow question (even undrafted) has the same effect. It's not about the duck; it's about converting implicit beliefs into explicit claims.

choices: Read the stack trace top-down: the exception type, message, and the first frames of YOUR code — the trace usually names the culprit
Stack traces are noise — start from main() and read forward
Only the last line matters — the rest is framework internals
Delete the try/catch — exceptions hide the real error
evidence:
System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set...
   at Shop.Orders.ApplyDiscount(Order o) in Orders.cs:line 42
   at Shop.Cart.Checkout() in Cart.cs:line 17
scenarios.hint: The trace lists the call chain at the throw point. Which frame is yours — and what does line 42 dereference?
scenarios.prompt: How do you read the stack trace?
scenarios.situation: A NullReferenceException with a stack trace; the developer doesn't know where to look.
scenarios.title: Reading the trace
scenarios.why: Read traces top-down: exception type + message (what), then frames (where) — the first frame in your code is the prime suspect (Orders.cs:42 dereferences something null). Framework frames below/above are context. The trace is the program telling you exactly where it gave up; ignoring it to read from main() discards the best evidence you have.

choices: Change three things at once — faster iteration
Change one thing, re-test, observe — single-variable experiments identify the cause; multiple changes confound the result
The fix is obvious — skip testing and ship it
Test only at the end — intermediate checks waste time
evidence: # three candidate fixes; developer applies all three, bug disappears
scenarios.hint: The bug is gone but you don't know which change fixed it — or whether two changes are now load-bearing. What experimental discipline was violated?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the 'fix'?
scenarios.situation: Three changes applied at once; the bug vanished, but nobody knows why.
scenarios.title: The fix that fixed unknown
scenarios.why: Changing one variable per experiment is how you learn the cause: apply fix A, test; revert, apply fix B, test. Three simultaneous changes confound the result — you can't distinguish the cure from the coincidence, and you may have added two unnecessary changes (or a masked second bug). Debugging is experimentation; single-variable discipline is what makes the conclusion valid.

choices: Everyone must use the same IDE — settings can't cross editors
Commit an .editorconfig defining indent, charset, and line endings — EditorConfig is supported across IDEs and enforces basics everywhere
Formatting can't be shared across different editors — accept the drift
Email everyone the settings — they'll apply them
evidence:
root = true

[*]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
end_of_line = lf
charset = utf-8
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
scenarios.hint: What travels with the repo and works in VS Code, IntelliJ, Visual Studio, and more — without anyone installing anything IDE-specific?
scenarios.prompt: How do you enforce the basics across different editors?
scenarios.situation: The team uses VS Code, IntelliJ, and Visual Studio; line endings and indentation drift.
scenarios.title: Three editors, one repo
scenarios.why: EditorConfig (.editorconfig at the repo root) is the cross-editor contract: indent style/size, line endings, charset, trailing whitespace — honored natively or via plugin by virtually every editor. It's the lowest common denominator that actually works. Deeper formatting (Prettier/Black) is per-language on top; EditorConfig covers the universal basics.

choices: Install a formatter (Prettier/Black) plus a linter (ESLint/Ruff) with shared configs committed to the repo — formatting automated, issues caught at write time
Formatting is personal taste — let everyone choose
Review formatting by hand in PRs — human eyes catch it best
Formatters slow down saving — disable format on save
scenarios.hint: Two tools: one rewrites code to a canonical style, the other flags probable bugs. What ends style debates forever?
scenarios.prompt: What is the baseline toolchain?
scenarios.situation: PRs drown in style comments; real issues get missed.
scenarios.title: The style-comment PR
scenarios.why: Formatter + linter with committed configs ends the debate mechanically: the formatter (Prettier/Black) makes style a non-issue by rewriting on save, and the linter (ESLint/Ruff) catches bug patterns, unused vars, and anti-patterns at write time. Style comments in review are the most expensive possible linter — automate them away and spend review on design.

choices: Everyone discovers extensions by word of mouth — curation is overhead
Commit .vscode/extensions.json with recommendations — new clones get prompted to install the team's extension set
Extensions can't be shared — each developer is on their own
Force-install extensions via group policy — recommendations are too weak
scenarios.hint: What's the lightest way to say 'this project expects these extensions' — so a fresh clone sets itself up?
scenarios.prompt: How does a new team member get the right extensions?
scenarios.situation: New hires take days to assemble the right extension set by trial and error.
scenarios.title: The onboarding scavenger hunt
scenarios.why: extensions.json recommendations prompt every fresh clone to install the team's extension set in one click — the project's tooling becomes self-describing. Word-of-mouth onboarding is lossy; forced installs are heavy-handed. Recommendations hit the sweet spot: visible, one-click, and versioned with the code they serve.

choices: Disable all telemetry immediately — it's all spyware
Review what each extension sends (many offer opt-outs), keep useful crash/usage telemetry for tools you trust, and disable or remove extensions that over-collect
Telemetry can't be disabled — accept it
Uninstall all extensions — only then is telemetry gone
evidence: # security review flags an extension phoning home
scenarios.hint: Not all telemetry is equal: crash reports that improve the tool vs. harvested code contents. What distinguishes acceptable from unacceptable — and who decides?
scenarios.prompt: How should the team evaluate it?
scenarios.situation: A security review flags an IDE extension sending telemetry.
scenarios.title: The extension that phones home
scenarios.why: Evaluate, don't panic: check what the extension actually transmits (network inspection, privacy policy), whether it's opt-out-able, and whether the value (crash reports, feature telemetry) justifies it. Extensions run with full user privileges — they're supply-chain surface. The policy: allow telemetry that improves the tool from vendors you trust, remove extensions that exfiltrate code or can't justify their traffic.

choices: Check the extension into the repo — vendoring is safest
Install from the marketplace and pin the version in the team's setup docs (or a lockfile where supported); review update changelogs for critical tooling
Always auto-update everything — newest is best
Extensions never have security issues — skip review
evidence: # a compromised extension version stole credentials last year (real-world supply chain attacks happen)
scenarios.hint: Extensions auto-update by default and run as you. What two controls — one about versions, one about review — reduce the blast radius?
scenarios.prompt: What is the sane update policy?
scenarios.situation: The team auto-updates all extensions without review.
scenarios.title: The auto-updating attack surface
scenarios.why: IDE extensions are privileged code with auto-update — a compromised release is a direct path to credentials (this has happened in the wild). Pin versions for critical tooling, review changelogs before updating, and prefer well-maintained extensions with many users. Auto-update-everything optimizes for features; pinned-and-reviewed optimizes for safety. Match the policy to the privilege.

choices: Use Settings Sync (built in) or a versioned dotfiles repo — your personal setup becomes reproducible and portable
Reconfigure manually on each machine — you learn the settings deeply
Screenshots of the settings UI — visual backup
Settings can't leave the machine — accept the loss
evidence: # new laptop; 40 extensions and 200 settings to recreate
scenarios.hint: Your setup is data. What makes data portable — a backup you can restore, or your memory?
scenarios.prompt: How should personal IDE setup be preserved?
scenarios.situation: A new laptop means recreating the entire IDE setup from memory.
scenarios.title: The setup that lived on one machine
scenarios.why: Settings Sync (built into VS Code, backed by your account) or a dotfiles repo versions your personal configuration — extensions, settings, keybindings, snippets — making any machine yours in minutes. Manual reconfiguration is slow and lossy; the project-level contract (.vscode/, .editorconfig) covers team needs, sync covers personal ones. Treat your setup as code.

choices: Alt+Tab to a separate terminal app — context switching builds character
Use the integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) — the shell lives next to the code, in the project's directory, sharing the editor's environment
The IDE has no terminal — that's what the OS is for
Terminals inside editors are slower — avoid them
evidence: # developer runs tests in an external terminal, then hunts for the failing file
scenarios.hint: The test output names a file:line. What happens if the terminal and the editor are the same app?
scenarios.prompt: Why use the integrated terminal?
scenarios.situation: A developer context-switches to an external terminal for every command.
scenarios.title: The alt-tab loop
scenarios.why: The integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) runs in the project directory with the editor's environment, and — critically — file:line references in output become clickable links that jump to the exact location. External terminals break that loop: see the error, alt-tab, navigate, find the file. Integration isn't about the shell; it's about collapsing the distance between output and code.

choices: Type the full build command from memory each time — memorization is a skill
Define tasks in .vscode/tasks.json (build, test, lint) with keyboard shortcuts — one keypress runs the project's standard commands
Tasks can't take arguments — they're useless for real builds
Write a README with the commands — documentation is enough
scenarios.hint: 'How do I build this?' should have one answer, runnable with one keypress. Where does the project store its command vocabulary?
scenarios.prompt: How should repetitive project commands be captured?
scenarios.situation: Every developer retypes the build/test commands from memory (slightly differently).
scenarios.title: The commands everyone retypes
scenarios.why: tasks.json (or npm scripts, Make targets, justfile) captures the project's command vocabulary as named, runnable, versioned entries — bound to shortcuts, composable (test depends on build), and identical for everyone. Retyped-from-memory commands drift; README commands rot. The runnable definition is the documentation.

choices: Run npm scripts directly — npx is redundant
Use npx (or the package manager's dlx) to run one-off binaries without installing — the right version, no global pollution
Install every tool globally — globals are the standard
npx only works for npm's own commands — not for project tools
evidence:
$ npx prettier --check .
# prettier isn't installed globally; still runs
scenarios.hint: The binary exists in node_modules/.bin but not on your PATH. What executes it without a global install?
scenarios.prompt: How do you run the project's local tools?
scenarios.situation: A developer installs every tool globally to run it.
scenarios.title: The global install habit
scenarios.why: npx resolves and runs the project's local node_modules/.bin binaries — the version the project pinned, not whatever's global. Global installs drift from project pins ('works for me' with prettier 2 vs the repo's 3) and pollute every project. Local-first execution (npx, or npm run scripts which add .bin to PATH) keeps the tool version tied to the repo.

choices: The shell is just a command runner — no learning needed
Learn shell editing (Ctrl+A/E to jump, Ctrl+R history search, !!/!$ reuse) — the terminal is an editor too, and fluency multiplies every command
Use only the up arrow — history search is advanced
Aliases are cheating — type everything in full
evidence: $ # developer retypes a 120-char docker command for the 5th time
scenarios.hint: Ctrl+R searches history; !$ reuses the last argument. What do these have in common — they treat your past commands as data?
scenarios.prompt: What shell skills pay off daily?
scenarios.situation: A developer retypes long commands from scratch every time.
scenarios.title: Retyping history
scenarios.why: Shell fluency — Ctrl+R reverse history search, Ctrl+A/E line jumps, !$ last-arg reuse, aliases for the 120-char docker invocation — turns the terminal from a typewriter into a tool. The commands you ran are searchable data; aliases version in dotfiles. Five minutes learning readline bindings pays back daily for a career.

choices: Keep the dotfiles in a git repo (bare repo or symlink farm in $HOME) — shell, git, and editor configs versioned, restorable, and diffable
Configure by hand on each machine — dotfiles are personal trivia
Dotfiles can't be versioned — they contain secrets
One giant .bashrc with everything — organization is overkill
scenarios.hint: Your shell config is code. What do you do with code — version it, or retype it?
scenarios.prompt: How should shell and tool configs be managed?
scenarios.situation: Each machine has a slightly different, hand-configured shell.
scenarios.title: The snowflake shell
scenarios.why: A dotfiles repo (git, often a bare repo in $HOME) versions shell aliases, git config, prompt, and tool settings — new machines converge in minutes, changes are diffable and revertable, secrets stay out (use a separate encrypted store). Hand-configured shells drift until 'works on my machine' includes the shell itself.

choices: Run the command and hope — output is output
Pipe through the right tool: grep for filtering, jq for JSON, less for paging, tee for capturing — compose small tools instead of scrolling
The terminal can't process output — copy it to an editor
Bigger monitors solve output overload
evidence: $ kubectl get pods -A  # 400 lines scroll past
scenarios.hint: 400 lines scrolled by. What Unix philosophy turns 'scroll and squint' into 'filter and see'?
scenarios.prompt: How should the output be handled?
scenarios.situation: A developer scrolls through hundreds of lines of command output.
scenarios.title: Scrolling through 400 lines
scenarios.why: Compose small tools: kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running isolates the problem pods; | jq '.items[].metadata.name' extracts JSON fields; | less pages; | tee captures while watching. The Unix pipeline turns firehose output into answers. Scroll-and-squint doesn't scale past a screenful — filtering does.

lessons.title: VS Code — Core concepts
concepts: Command Palette: the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) is VS Code's universal command launcher: type a few letters of any command — menu items, extension actions, settings — and run it without touching the mouse.
Keyboard-first navigation compounds: the palette removes the need to memorize dozens of individual shortcuts.
Launch.json in .vscode/ defines debug configurations: type (debugger, e.g. node/python), request (launch vs attach), program (what to run), plus args, env, and preLaunchTask.
Multi-cursor: for cross-file renames, F2 (rename symbol) is the language-aware tool — multi-cursor is for the local, mechanical case.

example.walkthrough: VS Code settings layer: user settings (personal defaults) < workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json, committed). Committing the workspace file makes format-on-save, the formatter choice, and rulers consistent for every clone — the repo carries its own editor contract. Personal preferences stay in user settings; project requirements go in the workspace file.

pitfalls: Common trap: the team must use the same OS for settings to apply.
Common trap: multi-cursor doesn't exist in VS Code.
Common trap: emmet only works in .html files.
Common trap: edit keybindings.json to add every command manually.

lessons.title: IntelliJ / PyCharm — Core concepts
concepts: Refactoring: shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed.
Rename: the IDE's refactoring engine exists precisely so renames are safe, previewable operations, not hope-driven edits.
Navigation: professional IDE fluency is largely navigation fluency.

Search Everywhere (double-Shift) finds classes, files, symbols, and IDE actions by name; Find in Path (Ctrl+Shift+F) searches file contents with regex and scope filters; Alt+F7 finds usages of the symbol at the caret.

Debugger: the debugger pauses at breakpoints and lets you inspect the full state: Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) runs arbitrary expressions in the current frame, Watches track values across steps, and conditional breakpoints stop only on the failing case.

example.walkthrough: Shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed. Find-and-replace is textual and blind.

pitfalls: Common trap: select the block and use Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M).
Common trap: run configurations can't take arguments.
Common trap: press Shift twice (Search Everywhere) or Ctrl+Shift+F (Find in Path).
Common trap: the IDE always runs the currently open file.

lessons.title: Visual Studio — Core concepts
concepts: Debugging: F5 = Start Debugging (debugger attached: breakpoints, variable inspection, slower startup); Ctrl+F5 = Start Without Debugging (just runs).
F5 vs Ctrl+F5: if you're not debugging, Ctrl+F5 skips the debugger overhead.
Attach to Process connects the debugger to an already-running process — breakpoints hit in the live service, with call stacks and variable inspection.
Immediate Window: the Immediate Window evaluates expressions and statements in the paused program's context — call methods, inspect objects, even assign variables to steer the session.
Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance.

example.walkthrough: Debug/Release are build contracts: Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance. Shipping Debug to production-adjacent environments is slower and can behave differently (timing, inlining). The dropdown also drives conditional compilation (#if DEBUG) — diagnostics code that must never ship.

pitfalls: Common trap: open the Immediate Window (Debug > Windows > Immediate) during a debug session and evaluate expressions / call methods in the current context.
Common trap: the Immediate Window only runs in Release builds.
Common trap: build configurations (Debug/Release) control symbols, optimizations, and conditional compilation.
Common trap: attach to Process only works for web apps.

lessons.title: Debugging Workflows — Core concepts
concepts: Reproduction: a reliable reproduction is the foundation: it turns 'sometimes' into a deterministic trigger, gives you a before/after oracle for the fix, and often reveals the cause while you minimize it.
Conditional breakpoints (break when order.Id == 7431, or when total < 0) stop only on the failing case; logpoints ('logpoints'/'tracepoints') print values without stopping at all.
Bisection is binary search on history: git bisect checks the midpoint commit, marks good/bad, and halves the range — ~9 steps for 300 commits instead of 300.

example.code:
System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set...
   at Shop.Orders.ApplyDiscount(Order o) in Orders.cs:line 42
   at Shop.Cart.Checkout() in Cart.cs:line 17
example.walkthrough: Read traces top-down: exception type + message (what), then frames (where) — the first frame in your code is the prime suspect (Orders.cs:42 dereferences something null). Framework frames below/above are context. The trace is the program telling you exactly where it gave up; ignoring it to read from main() discards the best evidence you have.

pitfalls: Common trap: bisect: check the behavior at the midpoint of the suspect range (git bisect for regressions, or halve the input), discard the innocent half, repeat.
Common trap: explain it to a rubber duck (or a teammate, or write it up).
Common trap: set a breakpoint at the loop start and press F5 10,000 times.
Common trap: understanding everything precedes any fix.

lessons.title: Developer Tooling - Core concepts
concepts: Editors (VS Code) are fast and extended via extensions; IDEs (JetBrains) bundle deep language understanding - indexing, safe refactoring, call hierarchies. Match the tool to the codebase size and language, not to habit.

Debuggers beat print statements for state you cannot see: breakpoints (including conditional ones), step over/into/out, watch expressions, and the call stack. Reproduce the bug first, then bisect with breakpoints.
Linters (ESLint, Pylint) catch bug patterns; formatters (Prettier, Black) end style debates. Run both in CI so the main branch is always clean and reviews discuss logic, not whitespace.

Git CLI is universal and scriptable - learn it first. GUI clients (GitHub Desktop, lazygit) shine at staging individual hunks and reviewing diffs; the concepts transfer because it is the same DAG underneath.
Dev containers and remote development (SSH, WSL) put the toolchain in version control. 'Works on my machine' dies when the machine is defined in a Dockerfile.
launch.json and tasks.json make F5 debugging and builds repeatable per project. Commit the portable parts; keep personal absolute paths out of shared config.

example.walkthrough: Install the formatter from the terminal so setup is scriptable, then pin format-on-save in workspace settings. Every contributor gets identical formatting without thinking about it - style becomes infrastructure, not discussion.

pitfalls: Common trap: debugging only with print statements - learn conditional breakpoints and watch expressions for intermittent bugs.
Common trap: committing .vscode/ with absolute personal paths - keep workspace settings portable or gitignore them.
Common trap: disabling a linter repo-wide to silence one noisy rule - use a per-line disable with an explanatory comment instead.
Common trap: resolving merge conflicts by picking one side for every hunk - read each hunk; conflicts often need a combination, then tests.

simulations.title: The breakpoint that never hits
simulations.brief: A breakpoint in app.ts never pauses the debugger. The code runs, the breakpoint stays hollow.

steps.symptom: Breakpoint shows as hollow (unbound); execution never pauses there.
evidence: Breakpoint ignored: no executable code at app.ts:42
options: Read the evidence: sourceMaps are off, so the debugger can't map app.ts:42 to the running bundle
The code has no bugs; remove the breakpoint
steps.explain: A hollow breakpoint means 'no executable code here' — with sourceMaps off, the debugger maps your TS file to nothing in the running JS bundle.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: source maps disabled in the launch config.
options: Enable sourceMaps in launch.json so the debugger can bind TS lines to running code
Set a breakpoint on every line
steps.explain: The compiler emits the maps; the debugger just needs permission to use them. One flag binds every breakpoint.

options: Confirm the breakpoint turns solid and pauses on the next run
steps.explain: Solid breakpoint plus a pause is the proof — the line mapping is working end to end.

simulations.debrief: Hollow breakpoints are mapping failures, not code failures. The compiler emits source maps; the launch config must enable them; the solid breakpoint is the proof.

simulations.title: Debug session setup
simulations.brief: Restore the order for setting up a debug session.

steps.context: Arrange the debugging setup steps in execution order.
items: Set a breakpoint on the suspect line
Choose the launch configuration
Start the debug session
Step through the code
Inspect variables at the pause

simulations.debrief: Breakpoint → config → launch → step → inspect. Skipping the config is how you debug the wrong process.

simulations.title: Quick fix or refactor?
simulations.brief: The editor offers two actions on a duplicated code block. Choose wisely.

steps.text: A 40-line block is duplicated in three files with small variations. The editor offers 'Extract Method' and 'Copy'. Which first?

choices.label: Extract Method: deduplicate first, then vary the parameter — one fix location instead of three
choices.feedback: Right: duplication is the bug factory. Extract first, parameterize the differences.

choices.label: Copy: faster right now
choices.feedback: Copying is how you got three divergent copies. Speed now, bugs later.

choices.label: Leave it — it works
choices.feedback: 'It works' three times is three places to fix the next bug.

steps.text: Extracted. The three call sites differ by one flag each. What next?

choices.label: Add a parameter for the flag — the method stays single-sourced
choices.feedback: Right: parameterize the variation, keep one implementation.

choices.label: Add three if-branches inside keyed on the caller
choices.feedback: Caller-sniffing inside the method recreates the coupling you just removed.

simulations.debrief: Duplication is the decision point: extract to a single source, parameterize the variation. Copy is never the fix for copy-paste.

simulations.title: The launch.json that misfires
simulations.brief: F5 does nothing: the debug session dies instantly. launch.json has 2 bugs in 12 lines.

issues.description: program points to srv/app.js but the built file is at dist/app.js — the debugger launches a file that doesn't exist.
preLaunchTask references 'npm: build' but the task is defined as 'build' — the pre-launch step never runs.
issues.fix: Rename the task reference to match the defined task label.

simulations.debrief: Launch configs are path contracts: program must exist where it claims, and task names must match exactly. F5 failing silently is always a config mismatch.

consoleSims.title: Bind the breakpoint
consoleSims.brief: app.ts:42 shows a hollow breakpoint. Enable source maps in the launch config from the IDE and rebind.

tasks.instruction: Open launch.json in the code editor.
tasks.hint: Find launch.json in the file explorer (the .vscode folder).

tasks.instruction: Set "sourceMaps" to true on the debug configuration.
tasks.hint: The flag lets the debugger map TS lines to running code.

tasks.instruction: Restart the debug session and confirm the breakpoint turns solid.
tasks.hint: Use the Run and Debug control.

consoleSims.debrief: Hollow → solid is the whole story: with source maps enabled, the debugger can bind your source lines to the running bundle.

consoleSims.title: Fix the task name
consoleSims.brief: The preLaunchTask 'npm: build' matches no defined task, so F5 skips the build. Fix the reference in the IDE.

tasks.instruction: Open launch.json in the code editor.
Change the preLaunchTask value to match the defined task label 'build'.
tasks.hint: Task references must match the task label exactly.

tasks.instruction: Press F5 (run) and confirm the build task executes first.
tasks.hint: Watch the task output before the debug session starts.

consoleSims.debrief: Task references are name contracts: a mismatch silently skips the build, and you debug stale code.

sections.heading: VS Code
items: Command Palette — the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) is VS Code's universal command launcher: type a few letters of any command — menu items, extension actions, settings — and run it without touching the mouse.
Keyboard-first navigation compounds — the palette removes the need to memorize dozens of individual shortcuts.
Launch.json in .vscode/ defines debug configurations — type (debugger, e.g. node/python), request (launch vs attach), program (what to run), plus args, env, and preLaunchTask.
Multi-cursor — for cross-file renames, F2 (rename symbol) is the language-aware tool — multi-cursor is for the local, mechanical case.
Common trap — the team must use the same OS for settings to apply.
Common trap — multi-cursor doesn't exist in VS Code.
Common trap — emmet only works in .html files.
Common trap — edit keybindings.json to add every command manually.

sections.heading: IntelliJ / PyCharm
items: Refactoring — shift+F6 Rename is a language-aware refactoring: it updates declarations, references, and (optionally) related files while respecting scope — a comment mentioning the old name isn't touched, a shadowing local isn't renamed.
Rename — the IDE's refactoring engine exists precisely so renames are safe, previewable operations, not hope-driven edits.
Navigation — professional IDE fluency is largely navigation fluency.

Search Everywhere — Search Everywhere (double-Shift) finds classes, files, symbols, and IDE actions by name; Find in Path (Ctrl+Shift+F) searches file contents with regex and scope filters; Alt+F7 finds usages of the symbol at the caret.

Debugger — the debugger pauses at breakpoints and lets you inspect the full state: Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8) runs arbitrary expressions in the current frame, Watches track values across steps, and conditional breakpoints stop only on the failing case.
Common trap — select the block and use Extract Method (Ctrl+Alt+M).
Common trap — run configurations can't take arguments.
Common trap — press Shift twice (Search Everywhere) or Ctrl+Shift+F (Find in Path).
Common trap — the IDE always runs the currently open file.

sections.heading: Visual Studio
items: Debugging — F5 = Start Debugging (debugger attached: breakpoints, variable inspection, slower startup); Ctrl+F5 = Start Without Debugging (just runs).
F5 vs Ctrl+F5 — if you're not debugging, Ctrl+F5 skips the debugger overhead.
Attach to Process connects the debugger to an already-running process — breakpoints hit in the live service, with call stacks and variable inspection.
Immediate Window — the Immediate Window evaluates expressions and statements in the paused program's context — call methods, inspect objects, even assign variables to steer the session.
Debug/Release are build contracts — Debug disables optimizations and emits full symbols for diagnosability; Release enables optimizations for performance.
Common trap — open the Immediate Window (Debug > Windows > Immediate) during a debug session and evaluate expressions / call methods in the current context.
Common trap — the Immediate Window only runs in Release builds.
Common trap — build configurations (Debug/Release) control symbols, optimizations, and conditional compilation.
Common trap — attach to Process only works for web apps.

sections.heading: Debugging Workflows
items: Reproduction — a reliable reproduction is the foundation: it turns 'sometimes' into a deterministic trigger, gives you a before/after oracle for the fix, and often reveals the cause while you minimize it.
Conditional — Conditional breakpoints (break when order.Id == 7431, or when total < 0) stop only on the failing case; logpoints ('logpoints'/'tracepoints') print values without stopping at all.
Bisection is binary search on history — git bisect checks the midpoint commit, marks good/bad, and halves the range — ~9 steps for 300 commits instead of 300.
Common trap — bisect: check the behavior at the midpoint of the suspect range (git bisect for regressions, or halve the input), discard the innocent half, repeat.
Common trap — explain it to a rubber duck (or a teammate, or write it up).
Common trap — set a breakpoint at the loop start and press F5 10,000 times.
Common trap — understanding everything precedes any fix.

Read traces top-down — exception type + message (what), then frames (where) — the first frame in your code is the prime suspect (Orders.cs:42 dereferences something null). Framework frames below/above are context. The trace is the program telling you exactly where it gave up; ign…

sections.heading: Extensions & Settings
items: EditorConfig — manual reconfiguration is slow and lossy; the project-level contract (.vscode/, .editorconfig) covers team needs, sync covers personal ones.
Team setup — extensions.json recommendations prompt every fresh clone to install the team's extension set in one click — the project's tooling becomes self-describing. Treat your setup as code.
Principle — it's the lowest common denominator that actually works.
Common trap — review what each extension sends (many offer opt-outs), keep useful crash/usage telemetry for tools you trust, and disable or remove extensions that over-collect.
Common trap — everyone discovers extensions by word of mouth.
Common trap — force-install extensions via group policy.
Common trap — formatting can't be shared across different editors.

sections.heading: Terminal & Tasks
items: Integrated terminal — the integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) runs in the project directory with the editor's environment, and — critically — file:line references in output become clickable links that jump to the exact location.

Tasks.json — Tasks.json (or npm scripts, Make targets, justfile) captures the project's command vocabulary as named, runnable, versioned entries — bound to shortcuts, composable (test depends on build), and identical for everyone.
Npx resolves and runs the project's local node_modules/.bin binaries — the version the project pinned, not whatever's global.
Common trap — use npx (or the package manager's dlx) to run one-off binaries without installing.
Common trap — define tasks in .vscode/tasks.json (build, test, lint) with keyboard shortcuts.
Common trap — alt+Tab to a separate terminal app.
Common trap — npx only works for npm's own commands.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For VS Code: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one IntelliJ / PyCharm lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Visual Studio terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
